specPoints.text: understand how selective breeding can develop plants with desired characteristics

primer.text: Plant breeders run the same choosing game as animal breeders, but on crops. This note defines artificial selection in plants, tours the features growers chase — from disease resistance to flower size — and then examines the hidden cost: repeatedly breeding the best-related plants narrows the gene pool and leaves a crop exposed.

lessons.title: Defining the Process and Its Crop Targets
lessons.opening: Artificial selection in plants means people, not the environment, pick the parents: individuals showing a wanted feature are crossed, their offspring are screened, and only offspring displaying the feature are crossed again. Growers chase disease resistance in food crops, bigger harvests, tolerance of drought or harsh weather, improved fruit flavour and larger or more striking flowers. One wild ancestor can even be sculpted into several entirely different vegetables.
keyPoints: Selective breeding in plants starts by crossing individuals that show a desirable feature.
Because not every seedling expresses the feature, offspring that do are chosen and re-crossed.
Many generations of this screening pass before a new variety reliably shows the feature.
Grower targets include disease resistance, higher yield, weather hardiness, better flavour and larger or unusual flowers.
Wild brassica was moulded by breeders into cauliflower, cabbage and broccoli, plus Brussels sprouts, kale and kohlrabi — six crops from one ancestor.

low.restatement: Cross the best plants, keep the seedlings that show the trait, cross again — many rounds until the crop is reliable.
low.analogy: Like picking only the fastest sprinters for relay training each season — after several seasons every runner on the team is fast.
low.examPointer: Name the loop: select, cross, select offspring, repeat — then quote at least two grower targets.

medium.restatement: Each generation, plants expressing the target characteristic are intercrossed while the remainder are discarded, so the alleles behind the trait rise in frequency until the variety breeds reliably.
medium.analogy: A seed catalogue that gets narrower every year: each reprint keeps only the pages gardeners actually order, until the catalogue is exactly what buyers want.
medium.examPointer: Anchor Higher-tier answers in allele language: selection raises the frequency of the desired alleles across the generations.

check.stem: What does artificial selection in plants begin with?

options.text: Crossing plants that show the wanted feature
options.explanation: Correct — the loop opens by crossing individuals that already express it.
Radiation mutagenesis is a different technique; artificial selection works with existing variation.
Laboratory gene transfer is genetic modification, a separate topic.

options.text: Growing plants in sterile tissue culture
options.explanation: Tissue culture is micropropagation, not the crossing loop of selection.

check.stem: Why is the crossing repeated after the first round?

options.text: Not every offspring shows the feature, so expressers are re-crossed
options.explanation: Correct — screening and re-crossing concentrate the trait generation by generation.

options.text: Seeds lose fertility after one season
options.explanation: Fertility loss is not the driver; the loop exists to filter offspring.

options.text: Each cross doubles the chromosome number
options.explanation: Chromosome number stays constant in normal crosses.
Inbreeding narrows variation; it does not create the wanted feature.

check.stem: Which target belongs to plant rather than animal breeders?

options.explanation: Correct — flower appearance is a classic plant-breeding target.
Temperament is an animal selection goal.
Wool quality belongs to sheep breeding.
Speed is a horse-breeding goal.

check.stem: Six familiar vegetables were all moulded out of one wild ancestor by breeders. Which group?

options.text: Cauliflower, cabbage and broccoli, plus Brussels sprouts, kale and kohlrabi
options.explanation: Correct — one wild brassica was moulded into six everyday crops.

options.text: Wheat, barley, oats, rice and maize
options.explanation: The cereal group has its own ancestry; the six named crops descend from brassica.
options.misconception: attributes the group to another ancestor

options.explanation: Orchard fruits are unrelated to the brassica group listed.
Root vegetables are not the brassica descendants named here.

check.stem: How soon can a grower claim a reliable new variety?

options.text: Only after many generations of selection
options.explanation: Correct — reliability is earned across repeated generational screening.
A first crossing only opens the loop; the variety is not yet reliable.
Germination says nothing about whether the feature is fixed.
One season cannot deliver a reliably breeding variety.

check.stem: State two features growers select for in food crops.
check.modelAnswer: Disease resistance and increased harvest size are two classic targets; hardiness to drought and better flavour are others.

check.stem: State the selector in artificial selection.
check.modelAnswer: The human grower chooses which plants cross, rather than leaving mating to natural agents.

check.stem: Explain why offspring screening matters in plant breeding.
check.modelAnswer: Because crossing desired parents does not guarantee every seedling shows the feature, growers must select the offspring that do and cross those again.

check.stem: A region needs a wheat line that survives drought. Outline a breeding plan.
check.modelAnswer: Cross the most drought-tolerant plants, grow the seedlings, keep and re-cross those that endure the driest trials, and repeat across many generations until tolerance is reliable.

lessons.title: Inbreeding and the Shrinking Gene Pool
lessons.opening: Chasing the 'best' individuals has a catch: the top performers are often close relatives, so pairing them is inbreeding. Each round of inbreeding trims the variety of alleles held by the population — the gene pool narrows. A narrowed pool raises the odds that a lineage inherits harmful defects and leaves it poorly armed against new diseases, because fewer resistant alleles remain in circulation.
keyPoints: Inbreeding means mating closely related 'best' individuals generation after generation.
The gene pool shrinks — the population holds fewer different alleles.
A reduced pool raises the chance of harmful genetic defects being inherited.
It also raises vulnerability to new disease, because resistant alleles are less likely to be present.

low.restatement: Breed only relatives, the gene pool shrinks, and defects plus disease risk climb.
low.analogy: A choir that recruits only from one family: everyone shares the same weaknesses, and one virus could silence the whole choir.
low.examPointer: Link the chain explicitly: inbreeding to smaller gene pool to more defects and less disease resistance.

medium.restatement: Restricting matings to related high performers removes allele variants from the population; with fewer alternatives, inheriting damaging recessives becomes more likely and resistance alleles spread less.
medium.analogy: An investment portfolio built only from one company's shares: any bad news about that company sinks everything, with nothing different to absorb the shock.
medium.examPointer: Quote the two consequences separately — inherited defects and disease vulnerability — for full marks.

options.text: Mating closely related individuals that show the desired feature
options.explanation: Correct — inbreeding pairs relatives selected as the 'best'.
Unrelated crosses widen the pool; they are the opposite of inbreeding.
Tissue culture is a propagation method, not a mating pattern.
Cross-species gene transfer is genetic modification.

check.stem: What happens to the gene pool under repeated inbreeding?

options.text: It shrinks, holding fewer allele versions
options.explanation: Correct — related matings strip variants out of the population.
Nothing in inbreeding adds variants; it removes them.
Restricted matings steadily reduce allele variety.
The pool's narrowing is exactly what weakens disease defence.

check.stem: Why does a narrowed gene pool raise disease risk?

options.text: Fewer resistant alleles are likely to be present
options.explanation: Correct — resistance depends on alleles the narrowed pool may have lost.

options.text: Diseases evolve faster in inbred crops
options.explanation: Pathogen evolution is not accelerated by the crop's inbreeding itself.
options.misconception: shifts the cause to the pathogen

options.text: The plants grow taller and attract fungi
options.explanation: Height is not the mechanism; missing resistance alleles is.
Insect carriage is unrelated to the gene pool's size.

check.stem: Which is a documented consequence of a reduced gene pool?

options.explanation: Correct — defect inheritance is the first documented consequence.
Yield gains were the selection goal; a narrowed pool brings costs, not automatic gains.
Photosynthesis rate is not a documented inbreeding consequence.
Novelty requires variation; the narrowed pool removes it.

check.stem: Inbreeding across generations trades which gain against which cost?

options.text: Human-valued gains bought at the cost of genetic diversity
options.explanation: Correct — that is the fundamental trade-off of the technique.

options.text: Diversity gains at the cost of slower change
options.explanation: Diversity falls rather than rises; the cost is diversity itself.
No immunity is gained; vulnerability to new disease rises.
Downsides are central: defects and disease vulnerability.

check.stem: State the term for all the allele versions present in a population.
check.modelAnswer: The gene pool — the collection of different alleles carried by the individuals of a population.

check.stem: State two risks that rise as the gene pool narrows.
check.modelAnswer: Inheriting harmful genetic defects and becoming vulnerable to new diseases are the two documented risks.

check.stem: Explain why breeders' 'best only' rule causes inbreeding.
check.modelAnswer: Because top performers tend to be closely related, repeatedly mating only them pairs relatives and narrows the pool.

check.stem: A rare wheat variety shows shrinking yields and rising disease hits. Diagnose the likely cause.
check.modelAnswer: Long selective breeding among related plants likely shrank the gene pool, so harmful defects accumulated and resistant alleles became scarce.

glossary.definition: Human choice of which plants cross, directing the features of the next generation.
A plant line produced by selection that reliably shows the chosen feature.
The full set of different alleles carried by the individuals in a population.
One version of a gene; different alleles give different forms of a feature.
Repeated mating of closely related individuals, which narrows the gene pool.
